definition: A material or substance that occurs in nature and can be used by humans. Examples include water, minerals, fossil fuels, and timber.
A resource that exists in limited quantities and cannot be replaced once used up. Examples include fossil fuels and metal ores.
A resource that can be replaced at the same rate as it is used, or is continuously available. Examples include timber (if replanted), wind, and solar energy.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Involves using resources efficiently and reducing environmental impact.
The process of converting waste materials into new materials and products. Reduces the need to extract virgin raw materials and conserves finite resources.
An analysis of the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life — from extracting raw materials, through manufacture, use, and disposal.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced during the life cycle of a product or by the activities of a person or organisation.
Water that is safe to drink. It is not pure water but contains dissolved substances at safe levels. Produced by treating fresh water or sea water.
A purification process in which a liquid is evaporated and the vapour condensed to remove dissolved substances. Used to purify water, especially sea water (desalination).
The removal of salt and other dissolved substances from sea water to produce potable water. Done by distillation or reverse osmosis. Energy-intensive and expensive.
A water purification process in which water is forced under pressure through a semi-permeable membrane, removing dissolved ions and particles.
A stage in water treatment in which particles clump together (flocculation) and settle to the bottom of the water, removing suspended solids.
A process that removes solid particles from water by passing it through a filter bed of sand and gravel. Used in water treatment.
The addition of chlorine (or ozone) to treated water to kill bacteria and other microorganisms, making it safe to drink.
The process of killing microorganisms in water using chlorine, ozone, or ultraviolet light. The final stage of drinking water treatment.
A technique for extracting metals from low-grade ores by growing plants that absorb metal compounds from the soil. The plants are harvested and burned to produce an ash rich in the metal compound.
A technique for extracting metals from low-grade ores using bacteria. The bacteria produce a solution (leachate) containing the metal ions, which can then be processed to obtain the metal.
An ore that contains only a small percentage of the desired metal. Traditional smelting is not economical for low-grade ores, so alternative methods like phytomining and bioleaching are used.
The traditional process of extracting metals from ores by heating with a reducing agent (such as carbon) at high temperatures. Not suitable for very reactive metals or low-grade ores.
The gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its environment, particularly with oxygen and water. Iron corrodes to form rust (iron oxide).
The corrosion of iron, producing hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Requires both oxygen and water to occur. Can be prevented by coating or alloying.
A method of preventing corrosion by attaching a more reactive metal (e.g. zinc or magnesium) to iron. The more reactive metal corrodes in preference to the iron.
Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting. The zinc acts as a physical barrier and also as a sacrificial metal, corroding in preference to the iron.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals or carbon). Alloys are harder and more resistant to corrosion than pure metals. Examples: steel, bronze, brass.
Hard, brittle materials made by heating clay or other minerals to high temperatures. Examples include pottery, bricks, and glass. Good thermal insulators.
Materials made of long chain molecules. Properties can be tailored for specific uses by changing the monomers or the conditions of polymerisation. Examples include polyethene, nylon, and PET.
Materials made from two or more different substances combined to give improved properties. Examples include carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) and fibreglass.
A hard, transparent material made by heating sand (silicon dioxide) with limestone and sodium carbonate. Soda-lime glass is the most common type.
A polymer that softens and melts when heated, and hardens again when cooled. The polymer chains are not cross-linked. Can be remoulded and recycled.
A polymer that does not soften when heated because the polymer chains are cross-linked in a rigid structure. Cannot be remoulded or recycled. Examples include Bakelite and melamine.
